marker_reviews.reason: The EXECUTE format() on line 210 is a read-only existence probe inside the BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE guard core.require_direct_support_for_canonical_edge(). It runs only while a row is being written, it creates, alters and drops no catalog object, and it writes no row, so a post-apply catalog assertion has no durable target to bind to. Its identifiers are not user input: they are the three literal trigger arguments written in this same migration, passed through format %s and %I quoting, so no untrusted text can reach the statement. The behaviour it implements - that an inferred or co-occurrence support edge can never sustain a direct canonical bridge row - is asserted instead in supabase/tests/canonical_licensing_relationship_bridges.sql, which runs against an ephemeral database on every pull request.

The two EXECUTE format() statements on lines 320 and 333 are read-only existence probes inside the DEFERRABLE CONSTRAINT trigger function core.assert_canonical_edge_still_supported(), which fires AFTER UPDATE OR DELETE on every support-edge table and is checked at COMMIT (round-2 review finding: a BEFORE row guard cannot see its own statement's effects on other rows, so one bulk withdrawal would pass row by row and commit an orphaned canonical edge). The probe on line 320 asks whether any canonical bridge row cites the pair carried by the OLD support row, using the bridge table name from tg_argv[0] through format %s and the two pair columns through %I. If none does, the trigger returns early. The probe on line 333 then asks, against the support-edge table itself named through %I.%I from tg_table_schema and tg_table_name, whether a CURRENT direct_source_assertion still names that pair; because it runs at commit the whole transaction is visible, so a same-source retire-then-replace inside one transaction is judged on its end state and is allowed to commit. Both statements only SELECT: they create, alter and drop no catalog object and write no row, so a post-apply catalog assertion has no durable target to bind to. Neither takes user input - the bridge table and the two column names are the literal trigger arguments written in this same migration, the support-edge table comes from the trigger's own tg_table_schema/tg_table_name, and both endpoint values are passed as USING bind parameters rather than interpolated - so no untrusted text can reach either statement. The function pins search_path to pg_catalog, pg_temp, is SECURITY DEFINER so it can read the catalog-of-record tables that the writing role need not be able to read, and revokes EXECUTE from public, anon and authenticated, so it is reachable only as a trigger. The behaviour it implements - that no statement shape may leave a canonical bridge row standing with no current direct source assertion under it, while supersession by replacement stays legal - is asserted instead in supabase/tests/canonical_licensing_relationship_bridges.sql steps 5d, 5d2, 5e and 5f2, which run against an ephemeral database on every pull request.

The EXECUTE format() on line 446 is a read-only single-column lookup inside the BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE guard core.require_support_edge_licensor_matches_endpoints(), added to close the round-3 review finding that a support row's licensor_id was NOT NULL and in the identity key yet tied to nothing, so a loader could file one licensor's endpoint pair under another licensor's id with no error. The guard is scoped to writes that actually set the columns it governs (round-6 review finding): on UPDATE it first compares the two endpoint references and licensor_id against OLD and returns early, running no dynamic statement at all, when none of the three changed. Without that early return an endpoint's later re-licensing - which is routine and permitted - would refuse every subsequent write to the historical support row, including its own documented withdrawal, so the stale assertion could never be retired. When the guard does run, it sits in a two-pass loop that reads the left endpoint's licensor_id and then the right endpoint's, and the row is refused when an endpoint declares a licensor different from the one the claim is filed under. It runs only while a support-edge row is being written, it creates, alters and drops no catalog object, and it writes no row, so a post-apply catalog assertion has no durable target to bind to. Its identifier is not user input: the endpoint entity table name is one of the four literal trigger arguments written in this same migration, passed through format %s quoting, and the endpoint id is a USING bind parameter. The function pins search_path to pg_catalog, pg_temp, is SECURITY DEFINER so it can read dam.asset for the service_role loader that holds no SELECT there (round-4 review finding), and revokes EXECUTE from public, anon and authenticated, so it is reachable only as a trigger. The behaviour it implements - that a claim's licensor must be the licensor its endpoints declare, whenever they declare one, and that a write touching none of the governed columns is left alone - is asserted instead in supabase/tests/canonical_licensing_relationship_bridges.sql step 6b, which runs against an ephemeral database on every pull request.
